claims.text: Greater initial atomic-scale disorder and kinetic arrest cause multi-element nanoparticles to preserve a single-phase, chemically mixed structure better during high-temperature service.
High-energy shock methods are used to synthesize high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Low-temperature reduction methods can produce the proposed near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
Rapid shock or low-temperature synthesis produces nanoparticles with a high density of grain boundaries.
Rapid shock or low-temperature synthesis produces a random elemental distribution.
A controlled moderate-temperature hold or slow-cooling treatment will partially equilibrate the nanoparticles relative to an untreated baseline.
Treated and untreated nanoparticles will be compared under identical catalytic-temperature and thermoelectric-temperature exposures in an inert or controlled environment.
An inert or controlled environment avoids extrinsic oxidation effects during the service exposure.
High atomic disorder and a high density of grain boundaries inhibit elemental diffusion and phase segregation.
Rapid synthesis creates a kinetically trapped, high-entropy state.
A random atomic distribution creates high diffusion barriers.
The proposed diffusion barriers retard elemental segregation at elevated temperatures.
Slow annealing reduces atomic disorder by permitting partial equilibration.
Annealing-induced equilibration lowers kinetic barriers and favors phase segregation.
Untreated nanoparticles will exhibit less phase segregation and better compositional stability after service than pre-annealed nanoparticles.
Pre-annealed nanoparticles will exhibit elemental clustering or secondary-phase formation during service.
The hypothesized stabilization applies only below the temperature or exposure threshold at which bulk diffusion dominates.
Sufficiently prolonged exposure or temperatures exceeding relevant diffusion activation barriers can eventually cause kinetically trapped structures to segregate.
A lack of significantly greater segregation or ordering in the pre-annealed samples relative to the rapidly synthesized controls would falsify the proposed kinetic-arrest mechanism.
